title: Real Estate, Commodities and Alternatives
intro: Beyond stocks and bonds lie assets that are physical (property, gold, oil), private (unlisted companies and loans), or new (crypto). Some offer real diversification or inflation protection; many come with high fees, poor liquidity and returns that are harder to measure than they look. This page goes through each with the same question: where does the return come from?

blocks.text: Real estate

Property earns rent (the income yield) and capital growth, which over long periods has roughly tracked inflation plus a little for land in growing places. The key measure for an income property is its cap rate (capitalization rate):

Net operating income (NOI) is rent minus operating costs (maintenance, insurance, property taxes, management, vacancies), before mortgage payments. A building with \$60,000 of NOI bought at a 6% cap rate costs \$1 million. Cap rates are to property what earnings yields are to stocks: they rise when interest rates rise, pushing values down.

items: Your home is a consumption good as much as an investment: it saves you rent, but it is a single, undiversified, leveraged asset with high transaction costs (often 6 to 10% to buy and sell) and ongoing costs. Robert Shiller's index shows US house prices rising only slightly faster than inflation over the long run, before costs.

Rental property adds income and leverage, and a second job as a landlord. Return on your cash invested depends heavily on the mortgage: leverage magnifies both gains and losses, as many found in 2007-2011.

REITs (real estate investment trusts) are listed companies that own property (offices, apartments, warehouses, data centers, cell towers) and must pay out most of their taxable income (90% in the US) as dividends. They give liquid, diversified access to property, but trade like stocks: US REITs fell almost 70% from 2007 to early 2009.
Private real estate funds report smoothed valuations, which makes them look less volatile than they are (see 'appraisal smoothing' below).

blocks.text: Commodities

Commodities are raw materials: energy (crude oil, natural gas), metals (gold, silver, copper), and agriculture (wheat, corn, soybeans, coffee, cattle). A barrel of oil pays no dividend and no interest, so a commodity's long-run return comes only from its price change, which has roughly kept pace with inflation over very long periods. Most investors get exposure through futures contracts, and the return of a futures position is not the same as the change in the spot price:

blocks.tex: \text{futures return} \approx \text{spot price change} + \text{roll yield} + \text{interest on collateral}

blocks.text: When later futures cost more than nearer ones (contango, common when storage is plentiful), a fund that keeps selling the expiring contract and buying the next one buys high and lets the price converge down, losing money even if the spot price is flat. When later futures are cheaper (backwardation), rolling earns a positive yield. The United States Oil Fund lost most of its value in 2020 partly through this, and in April 2020 the expiring WTI crude contract briefly settled at −\$37 a barrel because storage was full. Gorton and Rouwenhorst (2006) found that a diversified, collateralized basket of commodity futures earned returns similar to stocks from 1959 to 2004, with low correlation to stocks and bonds and positive correlation to inflation surprises; returns since have been much weaker.
Gold

Gold produces no income. People hold it as a store of value outside the financial system, a hedge against currency debasement and extreme crises, and central banks hold it as a reserve. Its real price swings enormously: it rose from \$35 an ounce in 1971 to about \$850 in January 1980, then took until January 2008 to pass that level in nominal terms (and longer in real terms). Its strongest link is with real interest rates: when real yields fall, the opportunity cost of holding gold falls and its price tends to rise. Erb and Harvey's 'The Golden Dilemma' (2013) is a good sober survey. A small allocation (0 to 10%) can diversify a portfolio; as a core holding it has long dry spells.
Private markets

items: Private equity (PE): funds that buy whole companies, often with heavy debt (leveraged buyouts), improve or restructure them, and sell after three to seven years. Venture capital (VC) funds invest in young companies, expecting most to fail and a few to return many times their cost.
Private credit: loans made directly by funds to mid-sized companies, mostly floating-rate; it grew quickly after 2010 as banks retreated.
Infrastructure: toll roads, airports, pipelines, utilities: long-lived assets with often inflation-linked income.

blocks.text: Private funds lock money up for ten years or more, charge high fees (management fees of 1.5 to 2% plus a 20% share of profits), and report returns as an IRR that depends on the timing of cash flows. Studies disagree on whether average buyout funds beat equivalent public stocks after fees (Kaplan and Schoar 2005 found roughly no; later data suggests a small edge for buyouts in some periods and wide dispersion between managers). VC returns are dominated by a few top funds that ordinary investors can rarely get into.
Appraisal smoothing

Private assets aren't priced daily by a market; they are appraised a few times a year, and appraisers move slowly. The reported returns therefore look smoother than the real economic swings, making volatility and correlation with stocks look lower than they are. Unsmoothing the data (for example, assuming reported value is a weighted average of true value and last period's report) typically roughly doubles the measured volatility. Some investors value this smoothness as 'volatility laundering', but the underlying risk has not gone away.
Hedge funds

Hedge funds are lightly regulated pooled funds that can short, use leverage and trade derivatives. Strategies include long/short equity, global macro, event-driven (merger arbitrage, distressed debt), relative value and fixed-income arbitrage, managed futures (trend following) and multi-strategy platforms. Fees have come down from the classic 2-and-20 but remain high. The broad hedge fund indexes have trailed a simple 60/40 stock and bond mix since around 2009; in 2008 Warren Buffett bet \$1 million that an S&P 500 index fund would beat a basket of funds of hedge funds over ten years, and won comfortably. The industry's averages also suffer from survivorship bias (dead funds stop reporting) and backfill bias (funds start reporting after good early years).
Crypto assets

Bitcoin (launched 2009) is a digital asset with a fixed supply schedule (at most 21 million coins), recorded on a public ledger (a blockchain) maintained by a decentralized network. Ethereum adds programmable contracts. Stablecoins are tokens meant to hold \$1 by holding dollar assets. Since January 2024, US spot bitcoin ETFs have offered regulated access.

items: Return source: crypto pays no cash flow (staking rewards aside), so its price rests on adoption and on what future buyers will pay. Supporters see a 'digital gold'; skeptics see a speculative asset with no intrinsic value.
Volatility: bitcoin has fallen more than 75% from peak several times (2011, 2014, 2018, 2022) and its volatility has often been three to four times that of stocks.
Specific risks: exchange and custody failures (Mt. Gox 2014, FTX 2022), stablecoin collapses (TerraUSD 2022), hacks, fraud, regulation and lost keys.
Correlation: in sell-offs since 2020 it has often fallen together with technology stocks, so its diversification benefit has been weaker than hoped.

blocks.text: If you choose to hold crypto, size it so that losing 80% of it would not change your plans, and prefer regulated custody to leaving coins on an exchange.
Collectibles and other things

Art, wine, watches, cars, stamps: high transaction costs (auction fees of 20 to 30% are common), insurance and storage, no income, thin markets and returns hard to measure. Treat them as things you enjoy, with possible value, rather than as portfolio assets.
Practice

blocks.title: Cap rate
blocks.text: An apartment building earns \$180,000 a year in rent and has \$60,000 of operating costs. Similar buildings sell at a 5% cap rate. What is it worth? What happens to the value if cap rates rise to 6%?
solution: At 6%: $120000/0.06 = \$2.0$ million, a 17% fall with no change in rent. This is duration in property form.

blocks.title: Roll yield
blocks.text: Crude oil spot is \$80. The one-month future is \$80.80 and the market is in steady contango of 1% a month. If the spot price is still \$80 in a year, roughly what does a fund that rolls monthly lose, before interest on its collateral?
solution: Each month it buys at 1% above where the contract will converge, losing about 1% a month: $0.99^{12} - 1 \approx -11\%$ for the year, though the spot price didn't move. (Interest earned on the cash collateral offsets part of this.)

blocks.title: Leverage on a house
blocks.text: You buy a \$500,000 house with \$100,000 down. Over five years it rises 15% in value. Buying and selling costs come to \$40,000 in all. Ignoring the mortgage interest, rent saved and upkeep, what is your gain on your down payment?
solution: Price gain $= \$75{,}000$; less \$40,000 of costs $= \$35{,}000$, which is 35% on your \$100,000. Leverage turned a 15% price rise into a 35% gain; a 15% fall would have cost you \$115,000, more than your whole down payment.
